$comment: Alert policy (D2-06). Config, not code: this file is read from disk at runtime, so a severity
change, a dedupe-window change or a cap change alters the running system with no rebuild.
alerts.test.ts (AC 4) proves it by scoring one identical watchlist hit under two policy files.
THE RULE THAT SHAPES THIS WHOLE FILE: severity starts from the watchlist category and can only
be LOWERED by how weak the identification is. It is never raised by a model's opinion.
Why the ceilings exist at all, in one measurement: D2-01 measured 0 exact plate reads across a
120-instance hand-labelled sample of this estate, because only 3 plates were legible. D2-03
then correctly rejected all 15 strings the live run produced, including '757508300' — a
hoarding's phone number, and the single highest-confidence read of the entire run. An engine
that fires 'critical' on input like that is manufacturing certainty from noise, and the first
officer who follows one to a hoarding stops trusting the queue. docs/alerting.md section 4.
The same vehicle at the same camera inside one window is ONE alert with a sighting count,
not fifty rows. Camera-scoped on purpose: the same vehicle at a DIFFERENT camera is new
information — it is movement, which is the thing a control room is watching for.
byCategory is the ticket's ordering (wanted_person > stolen_vehicle > blacklisted_vehicle >
suspect > missing_person) expressed against the four-value alert_severity enum. Two
categories share 'high', so categoryRank carries the strict ordering the queue sorts on —
collapsing five categories onto four levels would otherwise silently lose it.
missing_person is 'low' as an ALERT severity and that is not a statement about how much a
missing person matters. It is a statement about what an ANPR hit on one is: a lead to follow
carefully, not a reason to intercept a vehicle. The rank keeps it visible in its own right.
$entrySeverityNote: 'ceiling' | 'ignore' | 'override'. Default 'ceiling': the severity a human put on the entry
caps the category default but cannot raise it. The officer who added the row knew something
the category does not — the five estate-ocr-output entries are seeded 'low' precisely
because they are OCR fragments, not registrations — and a category default must not shout
over that. 'override' would let the entry win outright; 'ignore' would use the category only.

identificationCeilings.$why: A fuzzy match is a ranked possibility. Nothing that might be a different vehicle gets to be the most serious thing on the screen.
A clean prefix of a registration is a usable identification and the dominant outcome on this estate — but it is missing characters, and the vehicle it names is a set, not one vehicle.

The read is not a registration under any Indian plate layout. It may still be worth looking at — the five seeded estate-ocr-output strings are exactly this — but it identifies nothing, and '757508300' is what the top of this distribution looks like.

$comment: maxDistance 2 is D2-04's measured operating point (docs/fuzzy-matching.md section 6): it
recovers GJ35U07 -> GJ35U0779 at weighted distance 0.70 and GJ32DD10 -> GJ32D0107 at 0.55,
and the measured false-positive count on unrelated queries is 0.
fuzzyRefusalCodes is the important line. A read D2-03 classifies as structurally non-plate —
all digits, all letters, empty, too short — gets maxDistance 0, which disables fuzzy search
for it entirely. Fuzzy-expanding a phone number invents neighbours that were never on any
vehicle. The EXACT path stays open for those reads, because exact string equality against a
watchlist entry is a fact rather than an inference — capped at 'low' by the
'ungrammatical-read' ceiling above, which is what keeps it honest.
$minPlateConfidenceNote: Raw OCR confidence floor, applied before any lookup. 0.25 rather than something comfortable
because the whole legible range on this estate is low: the five seeded estate strings were
measured at 0.449, 0.503, 0.732, 0.627 and 0.56. A floor at 0.5 would silence most of the
estate's real output and make the demo look better than the cameras are.

$comment: The cap is on DELIVERY, never on persistence. Every alert row is written to `alerts` whatever
happens here — suppressing evidence would be the worse failure. What is capped is the
operator's queue, because the thing that actually drowns in a camera storm is the human.
120/minute is two per second: fast enough that a real incident is never held back, slow
enough that a stuck feed re-detecting the same scene cannot fill a screen. Overflow is
aggregated into one `alert_digests` row per window plus one `digest` stream event, so the
operator is told what they were not shown.
Signed-URL lifetime for the crop on an alert. 15 minutes: long enough to open the queue,
read it and click through, short enough that a URL pasted into a chat stops working. The URL
is minted at read time and never stored — a stored signed URL is a credential with an expiry
rotting in the database (D2-02's handoff).
